metadata.title: On Some Sequences of Integers
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: metadata.json lists this as Roth 1953 'On Certain Sets of Integers' but the actual PDF at source/paper342.pdf is Erdős & Turán 1936 'On Some Sequences of Integers' (J. London Math. Soc. 11). The two papers are closely related (both concern A-sequences / Roth-type density bounds), but the registry entry is mislabeled.

nodes.name: A-sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence of integers $a_1 < a_2 < \dots \le N$ is an $A$-sequence (belonging to $N$) if it contains no three terms in arithmetic progression, i.e. no $a_i, a_j, a_k$ with $a_j - a_i = a_k - a_j$.
nodes.statement_clean: An A-sequence in [1,N] is a set of positive integers up to N with no three-term arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Maximum-length function $r(N)$
nodes.statement: $r(N)$ denotes the maximum number of elements of an $A$-sequence belonging to $N$.
nodes.statement_clean: r(N) is the size of a largest 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N}.

nodes.name: Generalized maximum-length function $r_l(N)$
nodes.statement: $r_l(N)$ denotes the maximum number of integers $\le N$ such that no $l$ of them form an arithmetic progression.
nodes.statement_clean: r_l(N) is the size of a largest subset of {1,...,N} containing no l-term arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Theorem I (density bound for A-sequences)
nodes.statement: For $N \ge 8$, $r(2N) \le N$.
nodes.statement_clean: For N at least 8, any 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,2N} has at most N elements.

nodes.name: Sharpness remark for Theorem I
nodes.statement: The bound $r(2N) \le N$ holds for $N = 4, 5, 6$ but fails for $N = 7$, so the hypothesis $N \ge 8$ cannot be relaxed to all $N$.

nodes.name: Theorem II (improved density bound for large $N$)
nodes.statement: For every $\epsilon > 0$ and $N > N_0(\epsilon)$, $r(N) < \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + \epsilon\right) N$.
nodes.statement_clean: For sufficiently large N (depending on epsilon), the largest 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N} has size strictly less than (1/2 + epsilon) N.
nodes.notes: The exact displayed formula in the PDF is partly garbled by OCR; reconstructed from the text remark 'we find that, for sufficiently large N > N(\epsilon), $r(N) < (\tfrac{1}{2}+\epsilon)N$. At present this is the best result for r(N).'

nodes.name: Reflection invariance of $A$-sequences
nodes.statement: If $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_r$ is an $A$-sequence in $N$, then $N+1-a_r < N+1-a_{r-1} < \dots < N+1-a_1$ is also an $A$-sequence.
nodes.statement_clean: Reflecting an A-sequence about (N+1)/2 yields another A-sequence.

nodes.name: Translation invariance of $A$-sequences
nodes.statement: If $a_1 < \dots < a_r$ is an $A$-sequence and $k < a_1$, then $a_1 - k < a_2 - k < \dots < a_r - k$ is also an $A$-sequence.
nodes.statement_clean: Translating an A-sequence by a constant yields another A-sequence.

nodes.name: Subadditivity of $r$
nodes.statement: $r(m+n) \le r(m) + r(n)$ for all positive integers $m, n$.
nodes.statement_clean: The maximum-length function r is subadditive.

nodes.name: Base-case values of $r$
nodes.statement_clean: Exact values of r(N) for N from 8 through 14 used as induction base cases.

nodes.name: $r(17) = 8$ and consequences
nodes.statement_clean: Exact value r(17)=8 propagates via subadditivity into a sequence of bounds doubling each step.

nodes.name: Further computed values
nodes.statement_clean: Exact values of r(N) for N=18,...,23 used to sharpen the recursion in the proof of Theorem II.

nodes.name: $A$-sequence achieving $r(41) = 16$
nodes.statement_clean: An explicit 16-element 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,41} matches the upper bound r(41) <= 16.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem I
nodes.statement: Induction on $N$: establish base cases $N = 4, 5, 6, 7$ (i.e. $r(8), r(10), r(12), r(14)$) by direct enumeration using reflection/translation invariance, then propagate via the subadditive inequality $r(2N) \le r(2N-8) + r(8) \le (N-3) + 4 = N+1$.

nodes.name: Reflection symmetry
nodes.statement: Observe that reflecting any $A$-sequence $a_1 < \dots < a_r$ in $[1,N]$ via $a_i \mapsto N+1-a_i$ yields another $A$-sequence (Lemma LP342.1).

nodes.name: Translation symmetry
nodes.statement: Translating an $A$-sequence by any integer $k < a_1$ also gives an $A$-sequence (Lemma LP342.2).

nodes.name: Subadditivity
nodes.statement: Splitting $[1, m+n]$ into $[1,m]$ and $[m+1, m+n]$ yields $r(m+n) \le r(m) + r(n)$ (Lemma LP342.3).

nodes.name: Base case $r(8) = 4$
nodes.statement: If $r(8) = 5$, by reflection/translation we may assume $1$ and two integers $\le 4$ lie in the maximum sequence, forcing $\{1,2,4\}$ or $\{1,3,4\}$; neither extends to a 5-element $A$-sequence in $[1,8]$. Since $1,2,4,5$ works, $r(8) = 4$.

nodes.name: Base case $r(10) = 5$
nodes.statement: If $r(10) = 6$, then $r(8) = 4$ and translation force $1, 2, 9, 10$ in the sequence; this excludes $3, 5, 6, 8$, leaving only $1,2,4,7,9,10$, which contains the AP $1,4,7$. Hence $r(10) \le 5$, and $1,2,4,9,10$ shows $r(10) = 5$.

nodes.name: Base case $r(12) = 6$
nodes.statement: If $r(12) = 7$, the same argument forces $1, 2, 11, 12$ and then $4, 9$ to occur; the resulting set $1,2,4,9,11,12$ admits no further extension, so $r(12) \le 6$. The sequence $1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 11, 13, 14$ gives $r(14) = 8$ and $r(13) = 7$.

nodes.name: Subadditive corollaries
nodes.statement: By subadditivity, $r(16) \le 8$, $r(18) \le 9$, $r(20) \le 10$, $r(22) \le 11$ – establishing the theorem for the special cases needed to start the induction.

nodes.name: Induction step
nodes.statement: Suppose the theorem holds for $2N - 8$. Then by subadditivity $r(2N) \le r(2N-8) + r(8) \le (N-3) + 4 = N+1$. Combined with the established base cases $N \in \{8, 9, 10, 11\}$, induction yields $r(2N) \le N$ for all $N \ge 8$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem II
nodes.statement: From $r(14) = 8$ deduce $r(17) = 8$ by case-analysis on whether $1, 17$ lie in a hypothetical 9-element sequence; iterate using subadditivity to get $r(2^{k+2} - 2^{k-1} - 1) \le 2^k - 1$, which gives the asymptotic bound $r(N)/N \to$ at most $1/2$. Refining via $r(20) = 8$ etc. tightens the constant to $1/2 + \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

nodes.name: Show $r(17) = 8$
nodes.statement: Since $r(14) = 8$, $r(17) \ge 8$. If $r(17) = 9$, then $1$ and $17$ must occur (else $r(14) = 8$ is violated), but then $9$ cannot occur (it would form $1, 9, 17$); applying translation gives $r(17) \le r(8) + r(8) = 8$.

nodes.name: Bootstrap to $r(34), r(35)$
nodes.statement: Subadditivity gives $r(34) \le 16$. If $r(35) \ge 17$, then $1$ and $35$ occur, excluding $18$ (the midpoint), so the same argument yields $r(35) \le 16$.

nodes.name: Iterate the doubling
nodes.statement: Repeating gives $r(71) \le 32$ and in general $r(2^{k+2} - 2^{k-1} - 1) \le 2^k - 1$, so $\limsup r(N)/N \le 1/2$.

nodes.name: Refinement
nodes.statement: By a similar but longer argument $r(18) = r(19) = r(20) = 8$, $r(21) = 9$ (with explicit witness $1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 16, 18, 19, 21$), and $r(22) = r(23) = 9$; iterating these refined inputs through the same doubling scheme yields $r(N) < (\tfrac{1}{2} + \epsilon) N$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $N > N_0(\epsilon)$.

nodes.name: Density conjecture for $A$-sequences
nodes.statement: It is probable that $r(N) = o(N)$, i.e. the maximum density of a 3-AP-free subset of $[1, N]$ tends to $0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Conjecture: any 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N} has size o(N).
nodes.notes: Resolved affirmatively by Roth (1953); the present paper only conjectures it.

nodes.name: Szekeres conjecture (case $l = 3$)
nodes.statement: Szekeres conjectured that $r\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}(3^k + 1)\right) = 2^k$. Verified for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$.
nodes.statement_clean: Szekeres' formula for r at the special values (3^k+1)/2.
nodes.notes: Now known to be false: refuted by Salem–Spencer-type constructions and by Behrend (1946) which gives much larger 3-AP-free sets.

nodes.name: Szekeres conjecture (general $l$)
nodes.statement: More generally, for any prime $p$ and the function $r_l$, $r_p\!\left(\tfrac{p^k - 2 p^{k-1} + 1}{p - 1}\right) = (p-1)^k$.
nodes.statement_clean: Szekeres' general conjectured value of r_p at a specific arithmetic argument.
nodes.notes: Exact formula partly garbled by OCR; reconstructed from the displayed equation on p. 264. Now known to be false in this strong form.

nodes.name: Conjectural quantitative van der Waerden bound
nodes.statement: Let $f(k, l) = N$ be the least integer such that every $l$-coloring of $[1, N]$ has a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression. The Szekeres conjecture would imply $f(k, l) \le l^{e^{k \log k}}$ (i.e. a much sharper bound than the original van der Waerden proof gives).
nodes.statement_clean: If Szekeres' conjecture holds, the van der Waerden number f(k,l) admits a much sharper upper bound than known.
nodes.notes: Stated as a consequence of CnjP342.2, not proved here. Bound expression is partly OCR-garbled.

nodes.name: Primes-in-AP consequence
nodes.statement: An immediate consequence of Szekeres' conjecture would be that for every $k$ there exist infinitely many $k$-term arithmetic progressions of primes.
nodes.statement_clean: Szekeres' conjecture would imply Green-Tao-style infinitude of k-APs of primes.

nodes.name: Lower bound via ternary expansions
nodes.statement: $r\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}(3^k + 1)\right) \ge 2^k$: take all $u < \tfrac{1}{2}(3^k - 1)$ whose ternary representation avoids the digit $2$; then $\{u + 1\}$ forms an $A$-sequence.
nodes.statement_clean: Numbers whose base-3 expansion avoids digit 2 form a 3-AP-free set, giving the lower bound 2^k for r at (3^k+1)/2.
